Al-Naḥḥās, Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Bursawī and Iṣlāḥī also give the circumstantial parse; al-Nasafī compares 'why are you standing?' {"id": "74:50/q05", "question": "How is مستنفرة read and understood?", "turns_on": "The fāʾ vowel determines active versus passive force; interpreters then differ over whether the active ist-form simply equals nafara or intensifies deliberate flight, and whether the next verse favors one reading.", "positions": [{"id": "74:50/q05/p1", "position": "With kasra on fāʾ, the asses themselves flee or take fright; istanfara can equal nafara.", "reasons": "Al-Farra calls kasra common and reports ʿĀṣim and al-Aʿmash; Tabari assigns it generally to Kufa and Basra and some Meccans; Farisi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Ashur, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nashr and others list its readers, with differing reports about individuals. Abu Ali al-Farisi and Abu al-Hasan prefer it because the following farrat says the asses themselves fled; al-Samin reports the same argument from some, but says an anecdote cannot invalidate a canonical reading. Ibn Khalawayh objects that fatḥa has no stated agent. Ibn al-Jawzi chooses kasra and cites al-Kisaʾi's poetic mustanfar, with Gharb a place. Wahidi, Razi, Qurtubi, Samīn, Bursevi and others compare nafar/istanfara with ʿajiba/istaʿjaba and sakhira/istaskhara; Farisi also compares these forms. Majaz distinguishes mustanfira, startled, from nāfira, fleeing; Ibn Qutayba cites a poet's fleeing ass for kasra. Al-Farra's cited verse, retold by Tabari, Thaʿlabi, Wahidi, Jishumi, Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, uses mustanfir of an ass, described variously as frightened or fleeing, and Jishumi says it follows she-asses westward. Abu Sawwar's Bedouin judgment, reported with variants of his name by Ibn Khalawayh, Farisi, Thaʿlabi, Wahidi, Tabrisi, Razi, Abu Hayyan, Samīn and Ibn Ashur, turns on hearing that the asses farrat min qaswara; some accounts say he first understood an agent or lion driving them and then chose the active form. Ibn Masʿud's nāfira variant also expresses flight."}, {"id": "74:50/q05/p2", "position": "With fatḥa on fāʾ, an external agent frightens or drives the asses to flight; the form is passive.", "reasons": "Al-Farra attributes fatḥa to Hijazis, and Ibn al-Jawzi reports it more common in Arab speech. Farisi, Thaʿlabi, Jishumi, Bagawi, Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, al-Nashr, Ibn Ashur and others give reader lists; Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and Medinese readers recur, while Abu Jaʿfar, al-Ḥasan, Abu Rajaʾ, Ayyub, and al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim appear in particular accounts. Nahhas reports al-Kisaʾi's two versions and reader lists differing in detail. Ibn Khalawayh and al-Samin explain the passive participle by an unstated frightening agent, identified as hunter, lion or archer; Ibn Atiyya says the pursuer's terror causes their flight, and Ibn Ashur says the next phrase identifies the cause. Abu ʿUbayd prefers fatḥa because istanfara implies another frightens the animals, a preference also attributed to Abu Hatim. Nahhas calls 'frightened' clearer and says the other form normally seeks an action, though it may figuratively mean fleeing. Wahidi lists istanfara, anfara and naffara as verbs for frightening an animal; Tabrisi transmits al-Zajjaj's poetic frightened asses as evidence for the open form. Qiraat-ER calls it a Pss passive participle."}, {"id": "74:50/q05/p3", "position": "The active form intensifies the asses' own flight: they seek, urge, or drive themselves into it.", "reasons": "Kashshaf says they seem to summon and urge flight themselves; al-Samin quotes Zamakhshari's vivid interpretation; Nasafi likewise depicts inward incitement. Jishumi distinguishes nufūr, departure in fearful agitation, from istinfār, seeking flight. Ibn Ashur says sīn and tāʾ intensify alarm and full-speed running. Bursevi sets the seeking-flight analysis beside the synonym analysis; Alusi prefers the intensive analysis over deriving it as simple 'fled'."}, {"id": "74:50/q05/p4", "position": "The readings are both acceptable or converge in describing frightened, fleeing asses.", "reasons": "Tabari accepts both established readings as sound; al-Farra says both forms are ordinary Arabic, supported by poetry. Abu ʿUbayda glosses both readings as frightened, while Ibn Qutayba calls the animals frightened and fleeing without assigning a vocalization. Majaz likewise distinguishes startled mustanfira and fleeing nāfira; Wahidi's concise gloss has startled, frightened wild asses. Tabrisi says the root of flight is uncovering or exposure, illustrated by a horse baring its teeth as it flees. Nahhas grants that the difficult active form can figuratively use istanfara for nafara; al-Samin warns that a Bedouin anecdote cannot cancel a transmitted canonical reading."}]}

{"id": "74:51/q03", "question": "What is the qaswara from which the asses flee?", "turns_on": "Reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and others differ, and sources cite Arabic usage, poetry, root derivation, animal behavior, and disputed Ethiopic vocabulary.", "positions": [{"id": "74:51/q03/p1", "position": "A lion.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra, al-Kalbī, Abū ʿUbayda, and others give lion; al-Wāḥidī records a black lion in Abū Hurayra's report. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported with both Arabic and Ethiopic lion glosses, with Persian shīr/shar and Nabataean ariyā/awiya equivalents varying across reports. Ibn Qutayba, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Bursawī, and others connect the name to qasr, overpowering beasts. Al-Māwardī cites al-Farazdaq; Abū Ḥayyān cites a poetic simile. Al-Ālūsī reports the majority of lexicographers for lion; Ibn ʿĀshūr notes Ibn Sīda's qaswar/qaswara pair. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the lion reading adds terror at Qurʾanic threats."}, {"id": "74:51/q03/p2", "position": "Archers, especially a group shooting at wild asses.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Mūsā, Mujāhid, Qatāda, ʿIkrima, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Muqātil, and others are reported. Mujāhid and al-Kashshāf specify a band; Qatāda says bows; al-Qurṭubī says they shoot the animals. Al-Baghawī and al-Azharī say the collective has no singular of its form, while some philologists reported by al-Qurṭubī treat qaswara as the plural of 'archer.'
